notes.meaning: Moses tells the Israelites that they are the children of the Lord their God. Because they belong to Him, they must not slash their bodies or shave their foreheads when mourning for the dead. Surrounding pagan nations practiced these painful rituals, but God's people were to show that their hope rested in the living God.

Israel was chosen by God to be His holy and treasured people out of all the nations on earth. Being holy means being set apart for God's special purpose and living in spiritual purity. Their daily behavior was meant to honor the God who chose them out of unearned grace.

God strictly commands His people not to eat anything that He has called detestable or unclean. What was clean or unclean was decided by God's command to keep His people distinct from surrounding nations. This rule taught them to practice obedience and holiness in every everyday meal.

Moses lists the four-legged animals that Israel was allowed to eat. These began with common livestock like cattle, sheep, and goats, which could also be used for sacrifices. They also included wild animals such as deer, gazelles, roe deer, and mountain sheep.

Any animal that has a completely divided hoof and also chews the cud was declared clean for food. Both conditions had to be met at the same time for an animal to qualify. God gave these clear physical signs so the people could easily know what to eat.

Animals that had only one of the two signs were forbidden as unclean. The camel, the rabbit, and the rock badger chew the cud but do not have split hooves. The pig has a split hoof but does not chew the cud, so Israel was forbidden to eat its meat or touch its dead body.

Water creatures were clean only if they had both fins and scales. Any sea creature lacking either fins or scales was unclean and could not be eaten. This excluded creatures like shellfish and catfish from Israel's diet.

Moses reminds the people that they are permitted to eat any clean bird. Clean birds were not listed one by one because they were common and widely recognized. Instead, the law focused on naming the smaller list of forbidden birds.

The law names specific large flying birds that were strictly forbidden, such as eagles, vultures, falcons, and kites. These birds are birds of prey or scavengers that feed on carcasses. God declared them unclean to protect His people and teach them spiritual separation.

Moses continues the list of forbidden birds with creatures like ostriches, various owls, gulls, and hawks. These animals were also hunters or scavengers of rotting flesh. God wanted His people to avoid animals linked with death and decay.

The list of unclean flying creatures concludes with desert owls, cormorants, storks, herons, hoopoes, and bats. These animals were regarded as unclean in their habits and unsuitable for God's holy nation. Even the bat, though flying like a bird, was kept out of the clean diet.

Flying insects that crawl on the ground were broadly declared unclean and could not be eaten. However, any clean winged creature permitted under God's law remained acceptable as food. This kept God's people careful about purity in the smallest details of life.

Israel was forbidden to eat any animal that died naturally, because its blood had not been drained in the proper way. They could give or sell such meat to foreign travelers who were not bound by Israel's covenant. The people were also commanded never to boil a young goat in its mother's milk, which rejected an unfeeling or pagan practice.

Every year the Israelites were required to set aside a tithe, meaning a tenth portion, of all their crops and farm produce. They were to bring this second tithe to God's chosen sanctuary and eat it in His presence during sacred feasts. Sharing this meal before God helped them learn to fear and respect Him constantly.

If an Israelite lived far from the sanctuary, carrying large amounts of bulky grain and livestock would be too difficult. God kindly allowed them to sell their tithe at home and convert it into silver. The worshipper could then tie the money in a pouch and carry it easily to the central place of worship.

Once at the sanctuary, the worshipper could spend that money on festive food and drink, such as beef, mutton, wine, or other celebratory beverages. The worshipper and their entire household were to eat and rejoice together in God's presence. God intended these holy occasions to be happy times that celebrated His goodness.

The Israelites were instructed never to forget the Levites living in their hometowns when celebrating these tithe meals. The Levites were set apart to serve the Lord and held no land inheritance of their own. God made His ministers depend on the people so both would support each other in worship.

Every third year, the entire tithe was stored in local towns rather than carried to the central sanctuary. This food was set aside to support the Levites, resident foreigners, orphans, and widows so that no one was left hungry. God promised to bless all their daily work when they cared generously for those in need.
